---
title: "Residual Correlation"
format: html
---

Repeated observations from the same experimental unit may remain correlated even after the mean structure and random effects have been modeled.

PGM provides first-order discrete and continuous-time residual correlation structures through the `nlme` framework [@nlme].

## Correlation Groups

Residual correlation is defined within the variables selected under **Correlation Groups**.

When more than one grouping variable is supplied, their order defines an outer-to-inner hierarchy.

For example, using the grouping variables from the Imperial Shag example dataset [@svagelj2021]:

`nestID`  
`chickID`

corresponds to a correlation grouping structure conceptually equivalent to

$$
\text{nestID}/\text{chickID}.
$$

When AR(1) or CAR(1) is selected, at least one Correlation Group is required.

Correlation Groups are independent of the Random Effects specification, although the two structures must be mutually compatible when they are used together.

## AR(1)

For observations separated by $h$ discrete measurement lags,

$$
\operatorname{Corr}
(\varepsilon_{i,t},\varepsilon_{i,t+h})
=
\phi^{|h|},
$$

where

$$
-1<\phi<1.
$$

AR(1) is most naturally interpreted when observations are ordered and approximately equally spaced.

The model describes correlation by discrete measurement lag rather than by arbitrary continuous temporal distance.

## CAR(1)

For observations made at times $t_{ij}$ and $t_{ik}$,

$$
\operatorname{Corr}
(\varepsilon_{ij},\varepsilon_{ik})
=
\phi^{|t_{ij}-t_{ik}|}.
$$

CAR(1) uses the actual temporal separation between observations and is therefore generally more appropriate for irregularly spaced measurements.

## Correlation without random effects

Residual correlation does not require a random-effects model.

If AR(1) or CAR(1) is requested without random effects, PGM fits the structure through generalized nonlinear least squares.

## Correlation with random effects

When random effects are present, PGM reconciles the random grouping hierarchy with the selected Correlation Groups.

A composite random grouping term may represent the same grouping unit as a sequence of correlation groups.

For example,

`species:replicate`

may be used as a random grouping unit while

`species / replicate`

defines the corresponding residual-correlation hierarchy.

The model is rejected when the random and correlation grouping structures cannot be represented by a compatible nested hierarchy.

## Random effects are not autocorrelation

Random effects and residual correlation represent different dependence mechanisms.

A random effect represents persistent differences among growth trajectories.

Residual autocorrelation represents association between observation-level departures occurring close together in time.

A model may require one, both, or neither structure.
